chordInfo.name: Sixth Chords
chordInfo.subtitle: Discover the warm, polished sound of sixth chords - a vintage harmonic color essential for jazz, swing, country, and Hawaiian music.

fundamentals.label: Definition
fundamentals.value: Four-note chords adding a major 6th interval to a major triad

fundamentals.label: Relationship
fundamentals.value: C6 contains the same notes as Am7 (C-E-G-A)

fundamentals.label: Sound Quality
fundamentals.value: Warm, resolved, polished - less tension than a seventh chord

fundamentals.label: Function
fundamentals.value: Tonic resolution, jazz endings, vintage color

applications.label: Jazz & Swing
applications.value: Standard tonic chord in jazz standards and big band arrangements

applications.label: Country & Western Swing
applications.value: Signature chord for classic country and pedal steel harmony

applications.label: Hawaiian & Surf
applications.value: Defining sound of slack-key guitar and vintage surf music

applications.label: Pop & R&B
applications.value: Adds sophistication and warmth to pop progressions

boxes.title: C6 (Major Sixth) Example
items: Root: C (1st degree)
Major 3rd: E (3rd degree)
Perfect 5th: G (5th degree)
Major 6th: A (6th degree)
Result: Warm, resolved sound with gentle color

boxes.title: The Am7 Connection
items: C6 = C-E-G-A, Am7 = A-C-E-G
Same four notes, different root
Context determines which name applies
Bass note and chord function decide the label
This interchangeability is key to jazz voice leading

boxes.title: Scale Relationship
items: Built from: Major scale degrees 1-3-5-6
The 6th replaces the 7th for a more settled feel
Common on I and IV chords in jazz progressions
Works beautifully as a final tonic chord
Creates less forward motion than seventh chords

voicingGroups.title: Open Position Sixth Chords
voicingGroups.tipDescription: These open voicings are the most common sixth chord shapes and a great starting point for adding sixth chords to your playing.

voicingGroups.title: Moveable Sixth Chord Shapes
voicingGroups.tipDescription: These barre-based shapes can be moved up and down the neck to play sixth chords in any key, giving you full fretboard coverage.

voicings.name: F6 (E-shape barre)
voicings.fingering: E-shape barre at 1st fret with 6th added
voicings.use: Jazz and bossa nova in F

voicings.name: Bb6 (A-shape barre)
voicings.fingering: A-shape barre at 1st fret with 6th added
voicings.use: Swing and big band in Bb

items.title: Jazz Turnaround: I6 - vi7 - ii7 - V7
items.description: A classic jazz turnaround using C6 as the tonic chord. Notice how C6 and Am7 share the same notes - the progression creates smooth voice leading through the cycle.

items.title: Country Swing: I6 - IV6 - V7 - I6
items.description: A bright country swing progression where sixth chords on I and IV create that classic vintage country sound, resolving through the dominant V7.

items.title: Vintage Jazz Ending: IVMaj7 - iv6 - I6
items.description: The classic jazz ballad ending. The IV to iv to I6 movement is one of the most beautiful cadences in harmony, ending on a sixth chord for warmth without tension.

items.title: Hawaiian Vamp: I6 - IV6
items.description: A simple two-chord vamp that captures the essence of Hawaiian slack-key guitar. Sixth chords are the signature sound of traditional Hawaiian music.

techniqueItems: Let all four notes ring clearly, especially the added 6th
Practice switching between a major chord and its sixth to hear the color change
Play C6 then Am7 back to back to internalize their relationship
Use a relaxed strumming hand for the characteristic warm tone
applicationItems: Replace any tonic major chord with a sixth for instant vintage flavor
Use sixth chords as smooth jazz endings instead of plain major chords
Combine with dominant sevenths for authentic swing and country sounds
Try alternating between the sixth and major seventh on the same root

practiceExercises.title: Practice Exercises
practiceExercises.tipDescription: These exercises will help you master sixth chords and integrate their warm, vintage sound into your playing across multiple styles.

exercises.title: Exercise 1: Major to Sixth Comparison
exercises.content: Progression: C - C6 - F - F6 - G - G6
exercises.detail: Play each major chord, then add the 6th to hear the tonal shift. Hold each chord for two beats and listen to how the added note changes the character.
exercises.tip: Focus on which finger adds the 6th and keep the rest of the chord ringing cleanly.

exercises.title: Exercise 2: Sixth and Minor Seventh Interchange
exercises.content: Alternation: C6 - Am7 - F6 - Dm7 - G6 - Em7
exercises.detail: Play each pair back to back. Since they share the same notes, practice hearing when the sound functions as a sixth chord versus a minor seventh by emphasizing different bass notes.
exercises.tip: Accent the bass note on beat 1 to establish the root and hear the chord identity shift.

exercises.title: Exercise 3: Swing Rhythm Comping
exercises.content: Progression: G6 - C6 - D7 - G6 (swing eighths)
exercises.detail: Comp through this country-swing progression using a shuffle feel. Focus on smooth transitions and keeping the swing rhythm steady with a relaxed right hand.
exercises.tip: Use a metronome with a swing setting and gradually increase tempo from 100 to 140 BPM.

concepts.title: Sixth vs. Seventh: When to Use Each
items: Sixth chords resolve and settle; seventh chords create tension and motion
Use a 6th on the I chord for a final, resting sound (C6 ending a tune)
Use a 7th on the V chord for forward motion (G7 pulling to C)
In jazz, I6 and IMaj7 are often interchangeable on tonic chords
Sixth chords avoid the half-step dissonance present in major seventh chords

concepts.title: Sixth Chord Variations and Extensions
items: Minor 6th (Cm6): Minor triad + major 6th - dark, dramatic sound
6/9 chord (C6/9): Adds both the 6th and 9th for a lush modern jazz voicing
Sixth chords can substitute for minor 7th chords (and vice versa)
In chord-melody arrangements, sixth voicings keep the melody note accessible
Walking bass lines pair naturally with sixth chord comping
